for elimination of x and y are

[latex]    \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R\left ( 1,3 \right )}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 10 & -2 & 1\\ 0& 4 & -3\\ 5 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} -4\\ 12\\ 34 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex] So the pivot for eliminating x is [latex]a_{11}=10[/latex]. Now to eliminate y, we need to compass the eliminate in second column at and below the diagonal. Since [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] is already larger in absolute value compares to [latex]a_{32}=1 [/latex] [latex] \therefore[/latex] The pivot elementfor eliminating y is [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] itself. [latex]\therefore[/latex] The pivots for eliminating x and y are respectively 10 and 4.
questions.explanation_html:
The equations are,
[latex] \begin{aligned} 5x+y+2z&=34 \\ 0x+4y-3z&=12 \\ 10x-2y+z&=-4 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The augmented matrix for gauss-elimination is,
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
Since in the first column maximum element in absolute value is 10, we need to exchange row 1 with row 3.
[latex] \left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 & 2\\ 0 & 4 & -3\\ 10 &-2 &1 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} 34\\ 12\\ -4 \end{matrix} \right ]\xrightarrow[]{R\left ( 1,3 \right )}\left [ \left.\begin{matrix} 10 & -2 & 1\\ 0& 4 & -3\\ 5 & 1 & 2 \end{matrix}\right|\begin{matrix} -4\\ 12\\ 34 \end{matrix} \right ][/latex]
So the pivot for eliminating x is [latex]a_{11}=10[/latex].
Now to eliminate y, we need to compass the eliminate in second column at and below the diagonal.
Since [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] is already larger in absolute value compares to [latex]a_{32}=1 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] The pivot elementfor eliminating y is [latex]a_{22}=4[/latex] itself.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] The pivots for eliminating x and y are respectively 10 and 4.

The degree of static indeterminacy of rigidity jointed frame in a horizontal plane
and subjected to vertical load only, as shown in figure below, is
questions.explanation: In general, total number of equilibrium equations for a 3-D rigidly jointed frame are 6. i.e. [latex] \Sigma F_{x}=0, \Sigma F_{y}=0, \Sigma F_{2}=0, \Sigma M_{x}=0, \Sigma M_{y}=0 [/latex] [latex] \Sigma M_{z}=0 [/latex] But for vertical loading, these equilibrium equations reduces to 3. I.e. [latex]\Sigma F_{y}=0, \Sigma M_{x}=0\text{ and }\Sigma M_{z}=0 [/latex] Also, at fixed support in a 3 -D rigidly jointed frame total number of external reactions are 6 i.e.. [latex] R_{x^{\prime}}, R_{y^{\prime}} R_{z^{\prime}} M_{x^{\prime}} M_{y^{\prime}} M_{z}[/latex] But for vertical loading, these external reactions reduce to 3 i.e., [latex] R_{y^{\prime}} M_{x^{\prime}} M_{z}[/latex] Thus for two fixed supports total external reactions will be 6 [latex] \therefore [/latex] Degree of static indeterminacy = Total external reactions - Total number of available equilibrium equations [latex] =6-3=3[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
In general, total number of equilibrium equations for a 3-D rigidly jointed frame are 6. i.e.
[latex] \Sigma F_{x}=0, \Sigma F_{y}=0, \Sigma F_{2}=0, \Sigma M_{x}=0, \Sigma M_{y}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Sigma M_{z}=0 [/latex]
But for vertical loading, these equilibrium equations reduces to 3.
I.e. [latex]\Sigma F_{y}=0, \Sigma M_{x}=0\text{ and }\Sigma M_{z}=0 [/latex]
Also, at fixed support in a 3 -D rigidly jointed frame
total number of external reactions are 6 i.e..
[latex] R_{x^{\prime}}, R_{y^{\prime}} R_{z^{\prime}} M_{x^{\prime}} M_{y^{\prime}} M_{z}[/latex]
But for vertical loading, these external reactions reduce to 3 i.e.,
[latex] R_{y^{\prime}} M_{x^{\prime}} M_{z}[/latex]
Thus for two fixed supports total external reactions will be 6
[latex] \therefore [/latex] Degree of static indeterminacy
= Total external reactions - Total number of available equilibrium equations
[latex] =6-3=3[/latex]
